title: Introduction to B Tree
description: The wide, shallow, self balancing tree that powers databases and file systems

sections.title: 3. The Rules That Keep It Balanced
8. B-Trees in Databases and File Systems
10. B-Tree vs BST vs Hash Table

blocks.text: A B-tree is a self balancing search tree designed to stay short and wide. Instead of one key per node, each node holds many keys and has many children, which keeps the tree shallow even when it stores millions of items.

This shape is not an accident. B-trees were invented for data that lives on disk, where the slow part is reading a block from storage. A short, wide tree needs far fewer of those slow reads than a tall binary tree.

blocks.caption: A B-tree packs many keys into each node, so the tree stays shallow
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655018-812989030.png

By the end of this topic you will understand why B-trees exist, how their nodes are structured, how search, insertion, and deletion keep them balanced, and why databases and file systems rely on them. It is one of the most practically important data structures in all of computing.

A useful analogy is a library catalogue. Rather than checking books one by one, you open a drawer that already narrows you to a small shelf. Each B-tree node is such a drawer: one look eliminates most of the data and points you to the right next drawer.
To understand B-trees, you must first understand the cost of reading from disk. Reading a block from a spinning disk or even a solid state drive is thousands of times slower than reading from memory.

blocks.caption: A tall binary tree needs one slow disk read per level; a wide B-tree needs very few
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655018-247183222.png
A balanced binary search tree storing a million keys is about twenty levels deep. Searching it could mean twenty separate disk reads, one per level, which is painfully slow.

A B-tree fixes this by making each node large, often the size of one disk block, holding hundreds of keys. With hundreds of children per node, a million keys fit in a tree only two or three levels deep, so a search takes only two or three disk reads.

items: Disk reads are far slower than memory access
A binary tree is tall, so it needs many reads per search
A B-tree node is wide and holds many keys
Fewer levels means dramatically fewer disk reads

blocks.text:
The whole motivation:

B-trees trade taller structure for wider nodes so that the number of slow disk reads per operation stays tiny, even for enormous data sets.

Put concrete numbers on it. Storing a million keys in a binary tree gives a height around twenty, so up to twenty disk reads per search. With a B-tree whose nodes hold two hundred keys, the same million keys fit in about three levels, so three disk reads.

That gap only widens as data grows. At a billion keys the binary tree is around thirty levels while the B-tree is still only four or five. On disk, where each level is a slow read, this difference is the whole ballgame.
A B-tree of a chosen order is a search tree where every node holds a range of keys and a matching set of children. The order sets how many keys a node may hold before it must split.
The keys inside each node are kept in sorted order. Between and around those keys sit pointers to children, and each child holds exactly the keys that fall in that gap.

blocks.caption: Keys in a node partition the range, and each child covers one interval
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655019-596213277.png

items: Every node holds keys in sorted order
A node with k keys has k plus 1 children
Each child covers the key interval between two of the parent keys
All leaves sit at the same depth, so the tree is perfectly balanced

blocks.text: That last property, all leaves at the same depth, is what makes a B-tree self balancing. No matter what you insert or delete, the tree never becomes lopsided.

The order, sometimes described through a minimum degree t, sets the limits. A node may hold between t minus 1 and 2t minus 1 keys. Choosing t large, so that a node fills a disk block, is exactly what makes the tree wide and shallow.

items: Keys within a node are sorted left to right
A node with k keys has exactly k plus 1 children
Child i holds every key between parent key i minus 1 and key i
All leaves share the same depth, so the tree is balanced

content.title: 3. The Rules That Keep It Balanced

blocks.text: A B-tree enforces a few simple rules on every node, and those rules together guarantee balance.

items: Every node except the root has at least a minimum number of keys, so nodes never get too empty
Every node has at most a maximum number of keys, so nodes never get too full
A node with k keys has exactly k plus 1 children
All leaf nodes are at the same level

blocks.text: The minimum and maximum are tied to the order. When a node would break the maximum, it splits; when it would break the minimum, it borrows or merges. Those two repairs, applied automatically, keep every leaf at the same depth.

Balance for free:

You never manually rebalance a B-tree. The split, borrow, and merge operations during insertion and deletion keep it balanced as a side effect.

For example, with minimum degree t equal to 3, every non root node holds between 2 and 5 keys and has between 3 and 6 children. The moment a node would hold a sixth key it splits, and the moment it drops below 2 keys it borrows or merges.
Searching mirrors a binary search tree, but at each node you scan among several keys instead of comparing to just one.

blocks.caption: At each node, find where the key fits and descend into the matching child
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655019-440314751.png

At a node, you find the position where your key would fit among the sorted keys. If it matches a key there, you are done. Otherwise you follow the child pointer for that gap and repeat one level down.
Because the tree is only a few levels deep, this reaches any key in very few steps, and crucially in very few disk reads.

Trace a search for 15 in a node holding 10 and 20. Since 15 is greater than 10 but less than 20, you follow the child between them. One comparison step at each level narrows the search until you land on the key or fall off a leaf.
If the node is internal you descend; if it is a leaf and the key is not present, the key simply does not exist in the tree. Either way you touch only one node per level.
Insertion always begins by finding the correct leaf, just like a search, and adding the key there in sorted order. The interesting part is what happens when that leaf is already full.

blocks.caption: A full node splits, and its median key rises into the parent
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655267-669493230.png
When a node overflows, it splits into two. The middle key moves up into the parent, and the remaining keys divide into a left half and a right half. This is how a B-tree grows.

If the parent then overflows too, it splits as well, and the splitting can cascade upward. If the root itself splits, a brand new root is created above it, and that is the only way a B-tree grows taller.

items: Find the leaf and insert the key in order
If the node overflows, split it in two
The median key moves up to the parent
Splitting can cascade, and a root split adds a new level

blocks.text:
Growth from the top:

A B-tree gets taller only when the root splits. That is why every leaf always stays at the same depth: height changes happen at the root, uniformly for all leaves.

Walk through inserting into a full leaf holding 10, 20, and 30 when a fourth key arrives. The node splits, the median rises to the parent, and the leaf becomes two smaller leaves. The parent now has one more key and one more child, and if that overflows, it splits in turn.

items: Descend to the correct leaf as in a search
Insert the key in sorted position
If the node overflows, split and push the median up
Repeat upward, creating a new root only if the old root splits

blocks.text: Deletion is the trickiest operation, because removing a key can leave a node with too few keys, breaking the minimum rule.

blocks.caption: An underfull node borrows from a sibling, or merges when siblings are also small
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655268-307725737.png
When a node falls below the minimum, it first tries to borrow a key from an adjacent sibling that has spare keys. The borrowed key moves through the parent to keep everything sorted.

If neighbouring siblings are also at the minimum, the node instead merges with a sibling, pulling a key down from the parent to join them. Like splitting, merging can cascade upward, and if the root loses its last key, the tree shrinks by one level.

items: Removing a key may leave a node underfull
Borrow a key from a sibling with spare keys if possible
Otherwise merge with a sibling and pull a parent key down
Merging can cascade, and can shrink the tree from the root

blocks.text: As a concrete case, deleting a key that leaves a node with too few keys next to a rich sibling triggers a borrow: a key rotates up from the sibling into the parent, and a key rotates down from the parent into the needy node, restoring the minimum without a merge.

items: Find and remove the key
If a node dips below the minimum, try to borrow from a sibling
If neighbours cannot spare a key, merge with one
A merge that empties the root removes a level

blocks.text: The magic of a B-tree is how slowly its height grows. Because every node has many children, the number of keys explodes with each level.
If each node has around t children, then a tree of height h holds on the order of t to the power h keys. Turning that around, the height is only about the logarithm of n in base t.
With t in the hundreds, that base is huge, so even a billion keys sits in a tree just three or four levels tall. This is precisely why so few disk reads are needed per operation.

Logarithm with a big base:

A binary tree has height log base 2 of n. A B-tree has height log base t of n, where t is large. A bigger base means a much smaller height for the same number of keys.

As a rule of thumb, if each node holds around b keys, then each extra level multiplies the capacity by roughly b. Since b can be in the hundreds, three levels already reach into the millions and four levels into the billions.

This is the single most important takeaway about B-trees: their height grows like the logarithm of n in a very large base, which is why they stay only a few levels deep for even the largest data sets.

content.title: 8. B-Trees in Databases and File Systems

blocks.text: B-trees and their close relatives are the backbone of systems that store data on disk. When you create an index in a relational database, it is almost always a B-tree behind the scenes.

items: Relational database indexes, which speed up lookups and range queries
File systems, which use B-trees to locate files and blocks
Key value stores that need ordered, on disk data
Any system where data is too large for memory and lives on disk

blocks.text: The reason is always the same: B-trees minimise the number of slow storage accesses while keeping the data sorted so that both exact lookups and range scans are efficient.

Ordering is the other reason databases love them. Because keys stay sorted, a B-tree index answers not only exact lookups but also range queries, like all values between two bounds, by walking a contiguous slice of the tree.

This is why almost every relational database builds its indexes as B-trees or B+ trees. They give fast point lookups, fast range scans, and predictable performance even as the table grows to billions of rows.
All the main operations on a B-tree share the same efficient bound, because they all walk a path of the tiny height.

items: Search: O(log n), following one path from root to leaf
Insertion: O(log n), including any splits along the path
Deletion: O(log n), including any borrows or merges
Space: O(n) to store the keys, with each node partly filled

blocks.text: The key point is that the logarithm is in a large base, so in practice the height, and therefore the disk reads, is just a handful.

Constant factors matter here:

Two structures can both be O(log n), yet the B-tree wins on disk because its logarithm has a huge base. Always weigh the real cost of a level, not just the big O.

content.title: 10. B-Tree vs BST vs Hash Table

blocks.text: It helps to place the B-tree next to the other search structures to see when each one wins.

blocks.caption: Hash tables for fast unordered lookups, BSTs in memory, B-trees on disk
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655269-184735631.png
blocks.alt: B-Tree vs BST vs Hash Table

items: Hash table: O(1) average exact lookup, but no ordering and no range queries
Balanced BST: ordered and fast in memory, but too tall for disk
B-tree: ordered, wide, and shallow, ideal for data on disk
Choose a B-tree when data is large, ordered, and stored on disk

blocks.text: A quick rule: use a hash table when you only need exact lookups and order does not matter, a balanced BST for ordered data that fits in memory, and a B-tree for ordered data that lives on disk.
A few points regularly confuse people learning B-trees.

items: A B-tree is not a binary tree; nodes have many children, not two
The B does not stand for binary, and the tree is deliberately wide
Nodes are usually only partly full, which is normal and expected
The B-tree and the B+ tree are different; the B+ tree keeps all data in the leaves

blocks.text:
Do not confuse the height with a binary tree:

A B-tree looks tall on a small diagram, but with real orders in the hundreds it is astonishingly shallow. Never reason about it as if each node had only two children.
Another common slip is thinking a split makes the tree much taller. A split usually just widens the parent; the height grows only on the rare occasion that the root itself splits.
When a problem or design involves large, ordered data on disk, reason through it like this.

items: Ask where the data lives; if it is on disk, minimising reads is the priority
Recall that wide nodes mean a shallow tree and few reads
Use search by descending through the sorted keys at each node
Trust splitting on insert and borrowing or merging on delete to keep balance
If you also need efficient range scans, reach for the B+ tree variant

blocks.text: This framing is exactly what interviewers expect when they ask how a database index works under the hood.

A strong answer names the disk cost first, then explains that wide nodes keep the tree shallow, and finally mentions splitting and merging as the self balancing mechanism. That progression shows you understand why, not just what.
The B-tree is a cornerstone of real world systems for one simple reason: it respects the cost of disk.

items: A B-tree is a wide, shallow, self balancing search tree
Many keys per node means very few levels and very few disk reads
Insertion splits full nodes; deletion borrows or merges underfull ones
All operations run in O(log n) with a large logarithm base
It powers database indexes and file systems everywhere

blocks.text: Whenever you index a database or store sorted data too big for memory, remember that a B-tree is almost certainly doing the heavy lifting.
If you remember one image, keep the wide and shallow tree in mind, where each node is a full disk block and a search touches only a handful of them.
